lessons.title: Discussing the work of family members
lessons.objective: Discuss the occupations of family members, respecting turns and listening to others.
lessons.course:
In a discussion we share ideas: “My mother is a nurse. She works at the district hospital. She looks after sick people.” We ask questions: “Where does your father work?” “What does he use?”
Rules: wait for your turn, look at the speaker, do not interrupt, say “Excuse me” to speak.
lessons.model: Two adults discuss their jobs: what they do, where, which tools they use and why they like their work.
lessons.guided: In a group of four, each pupil presents one family member’s job in three sentences; the others ask one question.
lessons.exercise: What do we say before speaking when someone has just finished?
lessons.transfer: Interview a family member about his or her job.

practice.prompt: Match each worker with his or her work.
practice.answer: nurse: sick people; mechanic: cars; tailor: clothes.

practice.prompt: Which behaviour is good in a discussion?
Ask a question about a job.
practice.answer: For example: Where does your mother work?

lessons.title: Reading numbers from 501 to 1000 in words
lessons.objective: Read numbers from 501 to 1000 written in figures and in words.
lessons.course:
We read hundreds, then tens and units: 534 = five hundred and thirty-four; 708 = seven hundred and eight; 960 = nine hundred and sixty; 1000 = one thousand.
In British English we say “and” after the hundreds. We put a hyphen between tens and units: forty-two.
lessons.model: The adult reads prices in a carpenter’s workshop: “The stool costs six hundred and fifty francs.”
lessons.guided: Read ten number cards in words. Match figures and words.
lessons.remediation: Read the hundreds first, then the rest.
lessons.transfer: Read the prices of five items in a shop in words.

practice.prompt: Match the figures and the words.
Which number is “seven hundred and forty-three”?
Listen and write the number in figures.

lessons.title: Spelling: the apostrophe ’s for one owner
lessons.objective: Use the apostrophe ’s to show that something belongs to one person, and look up spellings in a dictionary.
lessons.course:
To show who owns something, we add ’s to the owner: the carpenter’s saw (the saw of the carpenter), the doctor’s bag, Mama’s shop.
Do not confuse with “its” (no apostrophe for ownership) and “it’s” (= it is).
When we are not sure of a spelling, we look it up in a dictionary in alphabetical order.
lessons.model: The adult writes: “This is the tailor’s machine. That is Ngwa’s scissors.”
lessons.guided: Rewrite ten phrases with ’s (the hammer of the builder → the builder’s hammer). Look up three words in a dictionary.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite with ’s: the car of the driver.
lessons.remediation: Start with names: Bih’s book, Tabi’s pen.
lessons.transfer: Label five things at home with the owner’s name and ’s.

practice.prompt: Complete with ’s.
Which one is correct?
Write three phrases with ’s about jobs.
practice.answer: Three phrases such as the baker’s bread.

lessons.title: Perfective tenses: has finished, had finished
lessons.objective: Use the present perfect and the past perfect to talk about completed actions.
lessons.course:
Present perfect: has/have + past participle — an action finished with a link to now: “The baker has baked the bread.” “I have finished my work.”
Past perfect: had + past participle — an action finished before another past action: “When we arrived, the shop had closed.”
Some past participles: done, gone, seen, written, eaten, made, taken.
lessons.model: The adult says: “The mechanic has repaired the car; you can take it now.” “When Papa came, the mechanic had already repaired it.”
lessons.guided: Make five sentences with “has/have” and two with “had”, about people at work.
lessons.exercise: Complete: The tailor … (finish) my dress. It is ready.
accept: The tailor has finished my dress
lessons.remediation: Learn the past participles of five verbs first.
lessons.transfer: Say three things you have done today.

practice.prompt: Match each verb with its past participle.
Complete.
practice.text: I [[have]] eaten. She [[has]] gone to the farm.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses the past perfect?
choices: The bus had left when we arrived.
practice.answer: The bus had left when we arrived.

lessons.title: Factors of a number: making equal teams of workers
lessons.objective: Find the factors of numbers and solve problems involving factors.
lessons.course:
A factor divides a number exactly. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (1 × 12, 2 × 6, 3 × 4).
A foreman with 12 workers can make teams of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12, with no one left over.
lessons.model: The adult arranges 12 counters in rows: 2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4… each arrangement gives a pair of factors.
lessons.guided: Find all the factors of 18, 20 and 24 with counters or multiplication facts.
lessons.remediation: Start from 1 and test each number up to half of the number.
lessons.transfer: Find in how many equal groups your family could share 24 oranges.

practice.prompt: How many factors does 16 have?
Which number is a factor of 15?
A carpenter has 20 planks to share equally among 4 workers. How many planks each?

lessons.title: Multiples and division: sharing the harvest
lessons.objective: Find multiples of numbers and divide by one-digit numbers, with and without remainders.
lessons.course:
Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30… (6 × 1, 6 × 2…). The multiples of a number are in its times table.
Division shares equally: 84 ÷ 4 = 21. Sometimes something is left: 50 ÷ 8 = 6 remainder 2. Check: 8 × 6 + 2 = 50.
lessons.model: The adult shares 96 cocoa pods equally among 3 baskets: 32 in each.
lessons.guided: Write the first ten multiples of 4 and of 7. Solve five sharing problems with remainders.
lessons.remediation: Use counters to share, then write the division.
lessons.transfer: Share a packet of biscuits fairly in your family and say the remainder.

practice.prompt: What is the 8th multiple of 9?
47 ÷ 5 = 9 remainder ?
Which number is a multiple of 7?

lessons.title: Money: shopping bills up to 5 000 francs
lessons.objective: Read and make shopping bills and calculate the total and the change up to 5 000 frs.
lessons.course:
A bill lists items, quantities, unit prices and totals. Line total = quantity × unit price. The bill total is the sum of the lines. Change = money given − total.
3 loaves at 200 frs = 600 frs; 2 tins of milk at 450 frs = 900 frs; total 1 500 frs. With a 2 000 frs note, change = 500 frs.
lessons.model: The adult acts a shopkeeper and writes a bill for three items, then gives the change.
lessons.guided: Make a bill for a family shopping list of four items. Calculate the total and the change from 5 000 frs.
lessons.exercise: Total 3 250 frs. You give 5 000 frs. What is the change?
lessons.remediation: Use play money to count the change from the total up to the note.
lessons.transfer: Check a real shopping bill with an adult.

practice.prompt: 4 bars of soap at 350 frs. Total in francs?
Bill: 1 200 + 850 + 1 450. Total in francs?
Write a bill with three items and its total.
practice.answer: A bill with lines and a total.
practice.explanation: Quantity × unit price for each line.

lessons.title: Bar graphs: the occupations of our parents
lessons.objective: Represent data on a bar graph and interpret it.
lessons.course:
A bar graph shows data with bars of different heights. It has a title, two axes with labels and a scale (for example 1 square = 2 people).
To read it: find the tallest bar (the most), the shortest (the least) and compare.
lessons.model: The adult draws a bar graph of the jobs of 20 parents: farmers 8, traders 6, teachers 4, drivers 2.
lessons.guided: Collect the occupations of the parents of ten classmates or neighbours. Draw a bar graph and write three sentences about it.
lessons.exercise: In the graph, which job has the tallest bar?
lessons.remediation: Make a table before drawing the bars.
lessons.transfer: Make a bar graph of the fruits your family eats in a week.

practice.prompt: Farmers 8, traders 6, teachers 4, drivers 2. How many parents in all?
How many more farmers than teachers?
Draw the bar graph of the four occupations.
practice.answer: A bar graph with a title, labels and a scale.

lessons.title: The fisherman’s tools and methods
lessons.objective: Identify the tools of a fisherman, describe fishing methods and the importance of fish in the diet.
lessons.course:
Fishermen use a canoe, paddles or an engine, nets, hooks and lines, traps (baskets) and a lamp for night fishing.
Methods: line fishing (a hook with bait), net fishing (casting a net or leaving it overnight), trap fishing (baskets in the river). Bad methods destroy fish: poison, explosives, nets with very small holes that catch baby fish.
Fish gives proteins for growth.
lessons.model: The adult describes fishing on the coast at Limbe or on a river: leaving at dawn, casting nets, selling the catch.
lessons.guided: Draw three fishing tools and say how each is used. Explain why poison fishing is forbidden.
lessons.exercise: Why are nets with very small holes bad?
lessons.remediation: Start with two tools: the hook and the net.
lessons.transfer: At the market, find two kinds of fish and ask where they were caught.

practice.prompt: Match each tool with its use.
practice.answer: hook: line; net: many fish; trap: river.

practice.prompt: Which method destroys the river?
practice.explanation: Poison kills all life in the water.

practice.prompt: What does fish give our body?

lessons.title: Raconter la journée du boulanger au passé composé
lessons.objective: Raconter des actions passées dans l’ordre en utilisant le passé composé.
lessons.course:
Le passé composé = avoir ou être au présent + participe passé : « Le boulanger a préparé la pâte. Il a cuit le pain. Il est allé au marché. »
Participes : préparer → préparé ; finir → fini ; vendre → vendu ; faire → fait ; aller → allé (avec être).
Pour l’ordre : d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin.

support.title: Lis le récit
support.text: Hier, le boulanger s’est levé à quatre heures. D’abord, il a préparé la pâte. Ensuite, il a cuit le pain. Puis il est allé au marché. Enfin, il a vendu tout son pain.

lessons.model: L’adulte raconte sa journée d’hier en levant un doigt pour chaque action.
lessons.guided: Raconte en cinq phrases au passé composé la journée d’hier d’un artisan (couturière, menuisier, mécanicien).
accept: Hier, il a vendu son pain
lessons.remediation: Travaille d’abord trois verbes en -er avec « avoir ».
lessons.transfer: Raconte en français ta journée d’hier à ta famille.

practice.prompt: Relie le verbe et son participe passé.
Remets le récit dans l’ordre.
items: D’abord, il a préparé la pâte.
Ensuite, il a cuit le pain.
Puis il est allé au marché.
Enfin, il a vendu son pain.
practice.explanation: Les mots d’ordre aident à raconter.

practice.prompt: Complète avec a ou est.
practice.text: Elle [[a]] cousu une robe. Elle [[est]] allée au marché.

lessons.title: Measuring the weather for farmers
lessons.objective: Use instruments to measure the weather, keep records and make simple instruments with local materials.
lessons.course:
Weather instruments: the thermometer (temperature), the rain gauge (rainfall), the wind vane (wind direction), the windsock (wind strength). Clouds also help to predict rain: dark, heavy clouds often bring rain.
Farmers need weather information to plant, spray and harvest at the right time.
A simple rain gauge: a clear bottle with a ruler scale, placed in an open place.
lessons.model: The adult makes a rain gauge with a cut plastic bottle and a ruler, then reads the water level after rain.
lessons.guided: Make a rain gauge and a wind vane with local materials. Record the weather each day for a week in a table.
lessons.remediation: Match three instruments with what they measure.
lessons.transfer: Share your weather table with a farmer in your family.
lessons.materials: Plastic bottle, ruler, cardboard, a stick.

practice.prompt: Match each instrument with what it measures.
Monday 12 mm, Tuesday 8 mm, Wednesday 0 mm of rain. Total in mm?
Draw your weather table for one week.
practice.answer: A table with days and weather.
practice.explanation: Write rain, sun, wind each day.

lessons.title: Seams and the chain stitch
lessons.objective: Sew a running stitch, a chain stitch and a plain seam on pieces of cloth.
lessons.course:
A seam joins two pieces of cloth. A plain seam: put the two pieces right sides together, pin them, sew a line of small running stitches about 1 cm from the edge, then open and press.
A chain stitch makes loops like a chain; it is used for decoration.
We cut a paper pattern before cutting the cloth.
lessons.model: The adult pins two pieces of cloth and sews a plain seam, then shows a few chain stitches.
lessons.guided: Cut a paper pattern for a small bag. Join two pieces of cloth with a plain seam. Decorate with chain stitches.
lessons.answer: It joins two pieces of cloth.
accept: it joins two pieces of cloth
It joins two pieces of cloth
lessons.remediation: Practise stitches on paper with holes before cloth.
lessons.transfer: Mend a small tear in a cloth at home with an adult.
lessons.materials: Needle, thread, pins, cloth, scissors, paper (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Put the steps of a plain seam in order.

lessons.title: Photographing a craftsman at work
lessons.objective: Describe the importance of photography and take photographs with appropriate focus to record an event.
lessons.course:
Photos keep memories, show events and inform people. A sharp photo is “in focus”. On a phone, tap the screen on the subject to focus, hold the phone still with two hands, keep the light behind you and fill the frame with the subject.
We always ask permission before photographing a person or a workplace.
lessons.model: The adult photographs a tailor at work (with permission): taps on the tailor to focus, holds still, then shows the photo.
lessons.guided: With an adult’s phone, photograph a person at work (with permission) three times: one blurred, one sharp, one close-up. Compare.
lessons.exercise: How do we focus on a subject with a phone?
lessons.answer: Tap the screen on the subject.
accept: tap the screen on the subject
Tap the screen on the subject
lessons.remediation: Practise holding the phone still with both hands.
lessons.transfer: Make a small photo story of a family member’s work.
lessons.materials: A phone or camera (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Which photo is in focus?
Match each tip with its reason.
pairs: hold the phone with two hands

practice.prompt: Write two sentences about the photo you took.

lessons.title: High jump: scissors technique
lessons.objective: Run, take off on one foot and jump over a bar using the scissors technique, landing safely.
lessons.course:
Scissors high jump: run up at an angle to the bar, take off on the foot farther from the bar, swing the inside leg up and over, then the other leg, like scissors. Land on your feet on a soft mat or sand.
Start with a low bar (a rope or elastic) and raise it little by little.
lessons.model: The adult shows the run-up at an angle and the scissors movement over a low elastic.
lessons.guided: Jump over an elastic at knee height, then a little higher. A partner holds the elastic loosely.
lessons.exercise: Why do we use an elastic instead of a stick at the beginning?
lessons.answer: So that we do not get hurt if we touch it.
accept: so we do not get hurt
so that we do not get hurt if we touch it
So that we do not get hurt if we touch it
lessons.remediation: Practise the leg movement while walking.
lessons.transfer: Play high jump with an elastic with friends safely.
lessons.materials: Elastic or rope, a soft landing area.

practice.prompt: Put the high jump in order.
The bar is at 60 cm. It goes up 5 cm each round. Height after 3 rounds, in cm?
Where do we land?
choices: on a soft mat or sand
practice.answer: on a soft mat or sand

lessons.title: Months and seasons in our language
lessons.objective: Use words for months and seasons in the family language in a conversation.
lessons.course:
Many Cameroonian languages name months or periods after activities and nature: planting, harvest, rains, dry wind, a festival. Seasons in much of Cameroon are the rainy season and the dry season; in the North the dry season is longer.
With an adult, we learn the family-language words for the seasons and some months or periods and what people do then.
lessons.model: The adult names the rainy and dry seasons in the family language and says what farmers do in each.
lessons.guided: With an adult, make a calendar of the year with the family-language words for seasons and two activities for each.
lessons.exercise: Name the two main seasons in much of Cameroon.
lessons.answer: The rainy season and the dry season.
accept: the rainy season and the dry season
The rainy season and the dry season
lessons.remediation: Start with the two seasons only.
lessons.transfer: Ask an elder what the old names of months mean.
lessons.materials: Paper, an adult who speaks the language.

practice.prompt: Match each season with an activity.
How many months are there in a year?
Draw your calendar of seasons with words in the family language.
practice.answer: A calendar with seasons and activities.
practice.explanation: Ask an adult for the words.

lessons.title: Special keys and shortcuts
lessons.objective: Use special keys of a keyboard and explain the importance of shortcuts.
lessons.course:
Special keys: Shift (capital letters and symbols), Caps Lock, Tab (indent), Enter, Backspace and Delete, the arrow keys, Ctrl and Alt.
Shortcuts save time: Ctrl + C (copy), Ctrl + V (paste), Ctrl + X (cut), Ctrl + Z (undo), Ctrl + S (save).
lessons.model: The adult types a word, selects it, presses Ctrl + C, then Ctrl + V to paste it twice, then Ctrl + Z to undo.
lessons.guided: With an adult, practise five shortcuts in a text. Without a computer, play a matching game with shortcut cards.
lessons.exercise: Which shortcut undoes the last action?
lessons.transfer: Show an adult a shortcut they do not know.
lessons.materials: A computer (with an adult) or shortcut cards.

practice.prompt: Match each shortcut with its action.
Which key writes one capital letter?
practice.explanation: Hold Shift and press a letter.

practice.prompt: What does Ctrl + X do?
practice.explanation: Cut removes and keeps the text to paste.
